title: Resource Contention in Production

sections.title: Design Options for the Recommendation Call

html:
Resource Contention in Production

A new feature may require only a few lines of application code while adding substantial work to requests that already serve customers. That work competes for the database connections, request workers, and downstream capacity allocated to existing traffic. Estimating it requires more than confirming that the new call returns the correct data.

Baodium encountered this problem while introducing personalized recommendations on product pages. The downstream service was familiar and the initial requests succeeded. The release review had not estimated how many database connections the additional recommendation lookups would occupy at higher exposure.1

Shortly after ten on a Tuesday morning, the team released a new product-page feature: a short list of products chosen for each customer rather than the same list for everyone. For requests with personalization enabled, the page handler called Recommendation Service to obtain the list.2

The team enabled personalization for one percent of product-page requests. Exposure was controlled by a feature flag3 that the page handler checked before calling Recommendation Service. The release owner could increase the percentage through the configuration console, and each instance applied the new setting when it next refreshed its local configuration.

Each increase sent more product-page lookups to Recommendation Service. The release procedure, however, had no estimate of the additional demand at each exposure step or a stop condition based on the service’s available capacity.

During the initial exposure, error rates and product-page p99 latency were comparable to the preceding thirty-minute baseline.4 The release owner increased the percentage. More of the existing page requests generated recommendation calls.

A few minutes later, product-page p99 rose above its pre-release range, while the median was still comparable to its own baseline. The slower requests were taking more time, but page latency and errors had not reached the configured release-stop thresholds.

The site reliability engineer (SRE) supporting the rollout examined Recommendation Service. Handlers were waiting longer for database connections, although query-execution p99 had not increased. The SRE shared those measurements with the release owner. The release plan had no stop condition for connection-acquire time, and the owner continued increasing exposure.

Seventeen minutes after the first increase, the customer-facing latency alert fired. Some customers saw a loading indicator until they refreshed the page or abandoned it.

Synchronous Dependencies

Recommendation Service already supplied personalized content for the home page and optional recommendations during checkout. The engineers had reviewed the product-page integration a week earlier. Because the service was familiar, the discussion concentrated on the request fields and returned data. The review did not estimate how many additional lookups product-page traffic would send to each Recommendation Service instance.

The missing estimate combined three quantities: product-page requests per second, the share that requested recommendations, and the time each lookup occupied a database connection. The interface review established how to call the service. The release plan also needed this estimate to assess the demand at each exposure step.

Before the release, Product Page Service called Catalog Service, retrieved the product information, and constructed the page.

For requests with personalization enabled, the engineers added a recommendation call after catalog retrieval.

[
  language=Python,
  caption={The product-page handler with personalization enabled.}]
def get_product_page(user_id, product_id):
    product = catalog_service.fetch(product_id)

    recs = recommendation_service.get(
        user_id=user_id,
        product_id=product_id,
    )

    return build_response(product, recs)

The handler waited for the recommendation result before constructing the response. Although it already had the product information, it could not finish the page until the recommendation call ended.

When we add a synchronous dependency, its response time becomes part of the caller’s response time. For the sequential calls in this handler, one page request took approximately

\[T_{\mathrm{page}} = T_{\mathrm{catalog}} + T_{\mathrm{recommendation}} + T_{\mathrm{local}},\]

where each downstream duration includes the caller’s wait for that result, and \(T_{\mathrm{local}}\) covers the other work in the handler.

These durations belong to the same page request, so the page’s p99 must be calculated from complete page-request durations. Adding the downstream services’ p99 values would combine observations that may have occurred on different requests.

One page request produced two downstream calls, a pattern known as fan-out. If the calls were independent, executing them concurrently could reduce the time needed to obtain both results. Every enabled page request would still generate a recommendation lookup, so Recommendation Service would receive the same number of calls.

The product requirement determines whether the handler needs both results before responding. If customers can inspect a product without recommendations, the application can return the product information when the recommendation call fails. If both results are required, the engineers must budget time and resources for both.

At Baodium, the engineers had not defined a fallback before the rollout. A failure or delay in optional content could therefore prevent the customer from receiving the primary page.

Design Options for the Recommendation Call

The team had five options when personalization was proposed. Each changed the work sent to Recommendation Service, the freshness of the result, or what the customer would receive when the lookup could not finish.

One option was to issue the live recommendation call concurrently with the catalog call. Concurrent execution overlaps the Catalog and Recommendation waits, so the page gets faster. Recommendation Service still receives one lookup for each personalized page request, and its capacity had to be evaluated separately.

They could have made the call optional from the start, with a short time allowance and a page that renders without recommendations when the allowance expires. This is inexpensive to build, and it is what the team eventually adopted. The trade-off requires a product decision: how large a share of pages may render without personalization before the feature stops earning its place on the page. It also obliges the team to measure the fallback rate, because page latency can meet its objective even while recommendations fail on every request.

They could have precomputed recommendations for each customer on a schedule and had the page read a prepared result. This removes the live dependency almost entirely, and in exchange it converts a compute problem into a storage and freshness problem. Recommendations drift out of date between runs, the cost of computing them moves into a batch job with its own schedule and its own failure modes, and an empty cache after a restart can recreate the original demand in a single burst. Chapter 5 follows that exchange through to its consequences.

They could have assigned separate connection pools to product-page, home-page, and checkout traffic, which would prevent one caller from using another caller’s connection allocation. The database would still serve all three pools, so their combined demand would need a limit. Reserved connections might be idle while another caller queued. Chapter 9 examines that utilization tradeoff and the conditions for sharing spare capacity.

Or they could have kept the live call and provisioned more: a larger pool, more service instances, a bigger database. Sometimes this is the correct answer. When the shared database is the constraint, however, each additional service instance opens another set of sessions against the same server, and those sessions add contention there without adding throughput.

Comparing these options required an estimate of the connections the new workload would occupy. That estimate would help the team choose an allocation and test exposure limits. Freshness, recommendation delivery, and implementation effort would still influence the choice.

Connection-Pool Measurements

The first question during the incident was which part of the recommendation call was slow. Database queries appeared to complete as expected, but the page handler was waiting longer for recommendations.

Recommendation Service used a database connection pool, and each instance could assign up to 40 connections to concurrent lookups. A handler acquired a connection before submitting its query and returned the connection to the pool after completing its database work. When all connections were assigned, later acquisition attempts entered a queue.

Most pool libraries expose their internal counters, either on a metrics endpoint or through an administrative command. The SRE pulled those counters for one affected instance and got the following. The connection counts are a snapshot at the moment of inspection, and the durations summarize the preceding thirty seconds.

[
  caption={A connection-pool readout during the incident.}]
assigned_connections       40
idle_connections            0
pending_acquisitions       80

acquire_p99             600 ms
acquisition_timeouts     increasing
query_p99               within pre-release range
occupancy_mean           70 ms

All connections were assigned, and another 80 acquisition attempts were pending. Those handlers had not submitted their queries because they were still waiting for connections. The query-execution measurement covered a later part of the operation.

Recommendation Service recorded three intervals:

Connection acquisition.

From requesting a connection until acquiring one or ending the attempt with a timeout, cancellation, or another failure. The service recorded this duration in db_pool_acquire_seconds , separated by outcome.

Query execution.

From submitting the query on an acquired connection through retrieving the complete result, recorded in db_query_execute_seconds for this lookup.

Connection occupancy.

From connection assignment until return to the pool, recorded in db_connection_occupancy_seconds .

To relate these measurements to the customer experience, the SRE examined a trace, a record of the timed operations performed for one page request.

Catalog Service had sent the requested product information back to Product Page Service. Product Page Service then called Recommendation Service and waited for its response. Inside Recommendation Service, the handler spent approximately 600 milliseconds waiting for a database connection. After acquiring one, it used the connection for about 70 milliseconds before releasing it.

A timer covering acquisition through release would therefore record approximately 670 milliseconds. Most of that interval was spent waiting to begin database work. The database’s slow-query log records queries whose execution duration crosses a configured threshold, so it might contain no slow query corresponding to this delayed page.

Separate acquisition and execution measurements help an engineer decide which investigation to pursue. High acquisition waits with a fully assigned pool warrant examining connection use and incoming demand. Longer query execution warrants examining the database work itself, including execution plans, locks, and storage access. Both can occur during the same incident.

Connection occupancy answers a further question: how long was the connection unavailable to other requests? For example, a query could finish in 20 milliseconds, followed by 50 milliseconds of result processing before the handler released the connection. The pool entry would be assigned for the full 70 milliseconds.

Using SQL execution time alone would underestimate connection use in that example. It also suggests a possible design improvement. Application work that does not require the connection may be performed after release, reducing the time other handlers wait for the same pool entry.

The engineers compared assigned connections with database session activity to investigate where occupancy time was spent.5 Request traces helped them distinguish query execution, result processing, and work between statements. The timers included caller, instance, and outcome labels. These allowed the engineers to calculate occupancy for the affected instance and separate product-page lookups from existing callers. They also examined unfinished operations because a connection still in use had not yet contributed its final duration to the occupancy mean.

Connection Demand and Utilization

The team now knew that requests were waiting for connections, but the queue did not identify the cause. The pool might be too small for the arrival rate, or each lookup might occupy a connection for too long. The next step was to estimate connection demand from the measured rate and occupancy.

We can begin by estimating average connection occupancy. An estimate above 40 would exceed the configured pool under the stated workload. An estimate below 40 leaves a further question: can bursts or longer connection use still fill the pool? The acquisition measurements and workload distribution are needed to answer that question.

During a reasonably steady interval with few failures, the affected instance completed approximately 400 lookups per second, which included product-page traffic and the existing home-page and checkout calls. Each lookup acquired one connection once, with a mean occupancy of approximately 70 milliseconds.

The estimated average number of assigned connections was

\[400 \times 0.070 = 28.\]

Multiplying the connection-use rate by mean occupancy gives 28. This is an application of Little’s Law: average concurrency equals the rate at which work enters a measured boundary multiplied by its mean duration within that boundary. Chapter 2 develops the relationship further. Four hundred connection uses per second, each holding its connection for 0.070 seconds, means about 28 connections in use at any instant.

Both numbers have to come from the same pool, and at Baodium both describe one Recommendation Service instance. Pairing fleet-wide traffic with a single instance’s pool would overstate demand by a factor of twenty; using query duration where connections were held for longer would understate it. Where a service records only one of the two, add the missing measurement before the release, while the change can still be reconsidered.

Twenty-eight connections is 70 percent of the pool. That average leaves 12 unassigned and says nothing about how often all 40 are in use, which is the question the queue of 80 pending acquisitions had already answered. Explaining those waits needs two quantities the average omits: when arrivals cluster, and how widely occupancy varies.

The combined mean also depended on the caller mix. Table \(\ref{tab:ch01-caller-load}\) separates the contributions to the shared pool.

Completed lookup rates and estimated average connection use for one instance. The total occupancy is the rate-weighted mean.
Caller Lookups/s Mean occupancy Connections
Product page 395 70 ms 27.65
Home page 3 40 ms 0.12
Checkout 2 115 ms 0.23
Total 400 70 ms 28.00

We calculate each caller’s contribution using its own rate and mean occupancy, then add the results. An unweighted average of the three durations would give the low-volume callers too much influence. This breakdown is useful before adding a feature. It shows how much of the shared resource the new workload is expected to use and which existing callers may be affected. Checkout contributed little to average connection use, but its lookups entered the same acquisition queue as product-page requests.

Use the rate of actual connection assignments in this calculation. Requests answered from a cache contribute no database assignment, while one request may acquire connections several times.

Suppose 40 percent of the 400 lookups per second use a cache and skip the database. If the others each occupy one connection for 70 milliseconds, mean occupancy is \(240 \times 0.070 = 16.8\) connections. Retries that acquire another connection increase the assignment rate; several queries executed during one assignment instead increase its duration. Count those changes at the pool boundary before applying the calculation.

The practical habit is to instrument the acquisition itself rather than the request, so the counter increments exactly when a connection is taken from the pool. This gives the calculation a direct count of pool assignments instead of requiring an estimate assembled from request counters with different measurement boundaries. Because that distinction is easy to miss, Listing \(\ref{lst:ch01-instrument}\) shows one implementation, recording the three intervals using Prometheus client conventions. In this listing, the acquisition timer wraps only the wait, so pool waiting is recorded separately from query time, and the use counter increments at acquisition, so its rate counts connection uses.

[
  language=Python,
  label={lst:ch01-instrument},
  caption={The three measurements the capacity estimate needs. Histogram
           buckets are chosen around the expected values so the useful
           percentiles are resolvable.}]
ACQUIRE_BUCKETS = (.001, .005, .01, .025, .05,
                   .1, .25, .5, 1, 2.5)
HOLD_BUCKETS = (.005, .01, .025, .05, .1,
                .25, .5, 1, 2.5, 5)

ACQUIRE = Histogram(
    "db_pool_acquire_seconds", "Wait for a pooled connection",
    ["pool", "outcome"], buckets=ACQUIRE_BUCKETS)
OCCUPANCY = Histogram(
    "db_connection_occupancy_seconds", "Assigned to released",
    ["pool"], buckets=HOLD_BUCKETS)
USES = Counter(
    "db_connection_uses_total",
    "Connections taken from pool", ["pool"])
IN_USE = Gauge(
        "db_pool_in_use",
    "Connections currently assigned", ["pool"])

@contextmanager
def pooled_connection(pool):
    start = time.monotonic()
    try:
        # Record acquisition separately from connection use.
        conn = pool.acquire(timeout=ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT)
    except PoolTimeout:
        waited = time.monotonic() - start
        ACQUIRE.labels(pool.name, "timeout").observe(waited)
        raise
    waited = time.monotonic() - start
    ACQUIRE.labels(pool.name, "acquired").observe(waited)
    # Count connection acquisitions, not incoming requests.
    USES.labels(pool.name).inc()
    IN_USE.labels(pool.name).inc()
    assigned = time.monotonic()
    try:
        yield conn
    finally:
        try:
            pool.release(conn)
        finally:
            IN_USE.labels(pool.name).dec()
            occupied = time.monotonic() - assigned
            OCCUPANCY.labels(pool.name).observe(occupied)

With those measurements available, PromQL can calculate the estimate directly. The demand in this chapter is the product of the use rate and the mean occupancy, which in PromQL is

# Estimated demand: uses per second x mean occupancy
  rate(db_connection_uses_total[5m])
* (  rate(db_connection_occupancy_seconds_sum[5m])
   / rate(db_connection_occupancy_seconds_count[5m]) )

# Measured, for comparison
avg_over_time(db_pool_in_use[5m])

The two should agree closely. Where they do not, the gap is itself the finding: a connection held outside the instrumented path, or a second caller against the same pool.

The engineers also examined a five-second interval during which the same instance received approximately 560 offered lookups per second. If mean occupancy continued to be 70 milliseconds, offered connection load would be

\[560 \times 0.070 = 39.2.\]

This estimates demand under the stated arrival rate and mean duration. The pool could assign at most 40 connections, with additional requests queued or rejected. The steady estimate represented 70 percent of the pool, while the 560-lookups-per-second estimate represented 98 percent.

With all connections assigned continuously, the idealized completion ceiling at a 70-millisecond mean occupancy was

\[\frac{40}{0.070} \approx 571 \quad \text{lookups per second}.\]

This assumes that mean occupancy continues at 70 milliseconds and no other bottleneck reduces throughput. At 560 arrivals per second, the instance could complete approximately eleven more lookups than arrived each second while a queue existed. That surplus determines how rapidly accumulated requests can be processed. A mean occupancy of 72 milliseconds would instead give

\[\frac{40}{0.072} \approx 556 \quad \text{lookups per second}.\]

Requests would arrive faster than the estimated completion rate. A change in result size, lock waits, or application work before connection release could account for the two-millisecond increase.

At the steadier rate of 400 lookups per second, mean occupancy would reach 100 milliseconds before estimated average demand accounted for all 40 connections:

\[\frac{40}{400} = 0.100 \text{ seconds} = 100 \text{ milliseconds}.\]

The two-millisecond sensitivity therefore belongs to the 560-lookups-per-second workload. At either rate, uneven arrivals and variation in individual durations can produce acquisition waits before average demand reaches the configured limit.

For a design review, these calculations provide specific test conditions. The proposed integration needs testing at the expected arrival rate, during bursts, and with longer occupancy. The release decision depends on the resulting acquisition waits and customer response times.

The workload’s p95 occupancy was approximately 105 milliseconds. Multiplying that duration by 560 gives 58.8, but average concurrency requires a mean. The result establishes neither average demand nor a p95 connection count.

If the mean increased to 105 milliseconds, sustaining 560 lookups per second would require about 59 connections on average. That is an explicit hypothetical test condition. The configured pool would still assign at most 40.

The steady calculation used completed lookups, while the 560-lookups-per-second calculation used offered lookups. During overload, the engineers needed to account for offered work through completions, unfinished requests, rejections, timeouts, and other outcomes.

::: decision

**What would you change first?**

You are the release owner. Exposure is at 25 percent. Product-page p99 has risen above its pre-release range, while the median remains comparable to its baseline. Recommendation Service reports all 40 connections assigned, 80 acquisitions pending, acquire p99 at 600 ms, and query p99 unchanged. Completed lookups are running at about 400 per second with a mean occupancy of 70 ms. You can make one change now.

**Raise the pool from 40 to 80 connections on each Recommendation Service instance.**

**Add four more Recommendation Service instances behind the load balancer.**

**Set the personalization percentage back to zero.**

—

The estimate is \(400 \times 0.070 = 28\) assigned connections on average. It does not explain when the pool reached 40. The pending acquisitions show that the limit was reached, while arrival bursts and longer assignments are possible causes to investigate.

A permits up to 40 additional sessions per instance. It could reduce acquisition waits if the database can execute the extra work, but could also increase lock, CPU, or memory contention. The database measurements needed to evaluate that change are missing.

B similarly adds up to 160 possible sessions through four new pools. It reduces the request rate at each instance only if routing distributes the work across the larger fleet. The shared database still receives the lookup workload.

C directly reduces the additional product-page demand. Instances stop admitting those calls after receiving the updated flag, and admitted calls then need to release their resources. The team chose this action to restore the page path while investigating the pool. Customers received product information without personalization. The next release used bounded lookups and a product-only fallback to limit that loss.

:::

Queueing Across Service Boundaries

A boundary identifies where an interaction or measurement begins and ends; it might enclose a handler, a connection pool, or a service call. The same team may operate both sides. Across a service boundary, the caller and receiver execute separately, and a caller can continue occupying resources while it waits for the receiver. In this example, the page worker is assigned throughout the recommendation call, while Recommendation Service occupies a database connection for part of that call. Those intervals require separate measurements.

That is what happened here. In Baodium’s implementation, each unfinished page request occupied one slot from a bounded worker pool, and a worker waiting for recommendations could not accept another page request. The traced recommendation lookup used a database connection only after acquisition, but its page worker was assigned throughout the wait. As more lookups queued, fewer page workers were available for new requests.

A request waiting for a connection holds a worker in Recommendation Service and, behind it, a worker in Product Page Service, so one scarce connection pins two other scarce resources for as long as the wait lasts. Queueing at the pool therefore consumes capacity along the whole request path.

An asynchronous client changes one of these resource constraints. With non-blocking I/O the waiting request releases its thread, so the same instance can hold far more requests in flight for the same thread count. What it does not do is reduce the number of requests waiting. Each one still holds its request context, its buffers, and its place in the connection queue, so the ceiling moves from thread count to memory and to the connection pool itself. At Baodium that would have changed the symptom from worker exhaustion to a longer acquisition queue and higher heap use, with the same 400 lookups per second arriving at the same 40 connections.

The revised design needed an admission bound to limit accepted work and an acquisition timeout to limit each accepted request’s wait. A stalled pool illustrates why both controls are necessary.

Suppose all connections are assigned, none is released for 200 milliseconds, and acquisition attempts arrive at 560 per second. During that interval,

\[560 \times 0.200 = 112\]

new attempts could arrive without a connection becoming available. With a 200-millisecond acquisition timeout, those attempts would only begin reaching their individual timeouts at the end of the interval. Previously queued work would add to the count unless it expired or was canceled.

The earlier completion estimate assumed connections were continually returned at a mean occupancy of 70 milliseconds. Under those conditions, 560 arrivals per second would allow an existing queue to decrease by roughly two lookups over 200 milliseconds in the simplified rate calculation. The stalled-pool example assumes no returns during that interval.

An admission bound limits how much work the application accepts under either condition. Enforcing it requires an atomic reservation. If several handlers read a concurrency gauge and accept work in separate steps, they can all observe the same apparent free slot. A semaphore or equivalent mechanism reserves capacity as part of accepting the operation.

The caller also needs a defined response to rejection; for optional recommendations, it can return the product page without recommendation content. That allows the page worker to finish without another attempt against the constrained pool.

Timeouts and Retry Traffic

Some gateway deadlines expired before page handlers returned. Customers refreshed the page after several seconds without a response, and those refreshes created new requests. Each new page request generated another recommendation lookup, even when the earlier lookup was still waiting to acquire a database connection.

Reloads add work while the constrained resource is already near its limit. After one refresh, two lookups from the same customer’s session may compete for the same pool. The capacity plan must account for this additional traffic and for what happens to the original request after the browser disconnects.

The recommendation allowance needed to account for time already spent on the page request and time required to construct the response. Acquisition wait consumed part of that allowance. On cancellation, a queued acquisition needed removal, while an executing query required driver handling and cleanup before its connection could be reused.

A gateway timeout alone did not confirm that downstream work had ended. Automatic retries could add further work. For example, 400 logical operations per second with an average of two attempts would produce

\[400 \times 2 = 800\]

attempts per second.

Record one identifier for the logical operation and a separate identifier for each attempt, so that you can count attempts per operation. Chapter 8 develops the instrumentation needed to follow that work across services.

A refreshed page arrives as an ordinary new request with a new identifier. Nothing in that request links it to the abandoned page load. Linking the two requires deliberate correlation, such as a session identifier plus the product being viewed, and even then it is an inference. The practical consequence is that customer-driven load is easy to underestimate during exactly the conditions that produce it.

The response team set the personalization percentage to zero in the configuration console. Each instance stopped admitting new product-page lookups after refreshing its local flag value, which avoided a build and deployment, but configuration propagation still took time. For example, an instance polling every thirty seconds could use the old value until its next successful refresh. Calls already admitted needed to finish, be canceled, or reach an enforced deadline before releasing resources.

The flag controls whether the handler calls Recommendation Service:

[
  language=Python,
  caption={Disabling the lookup changes which branch executes, not which
           code is deployed.}]
def get_product_page(user_id, product_id):
    product = catalog_service.fetch(product_id)

    if not flags.enabled("page_personalization", user_id):
        return build_response(product, recs=None)

    recs = recommendation_service.get(
        user_id=user_id,
        product_id=product_id,
    )
    return build_response(product, recs)

The flag stopped new lookups. Work already admitted continued, and the 80 pending acquisition attempts still had to acquire a connection, time out, or be canceled. The 40 active assignments also had to finish before the pool could reuse those connections. Recovery therefore depended on how quickly the existing work completed. The engineers monitored the pending-acquisition count until it approached zero; lower page latency alone did not establish that the earlier queue had cleared.

Disabling the feature also removes recommendations from requests that were completing successfully. The release plan therefore needs a predefined threshold for using the kill switch, such as a sustained breach of the page-latency objective, rather than leaving that decision to the responder during the incident.

For the next release, the engineers removed automatic retries from the initial page path. Returning product information fulfilled the primary customer request, and another recommendation attempt would use more of the page budget and require another connection. Chapter 4 examines deadline and cancellation handling across service calls in detail.

Bounded Lookup and Degradation

The product lead and engineers agreed that customers could receive the product page without personalized recommendations when the lookup was unavailable. Product Page Service would attempt a live lookup for a defined portion of the page’s response budget. If admission failed, the lookup failed, or the allowance expired, the handler would return the product information without recommendations. The team accepted a delay of up to the lookup allowance when Recommendation Service stalled. During that interval, the page worker would still be assigned to the request. Customers could receive current recommendations when the lookup completed in time, and the engineers could test this change before undertaking a larger redesign.

The handler would skip the lookup when the remaining page budget could not cover both its allowance and response construction. Recommendation Service would enforce an admission bound and an acquisition timeout, and the caller would cancel unfinished work when its allowance expired.

This fallback skips the constrained Recommendation Service pool. A fallback that queries the same database through that pool would wait for the same connections. If it starts only after the primary attempt times out, it also adds another wait to the page response. Check the resources each fallback uses under the specific failure it is intended to handle.

Home pages would likewise omit unavailable recommendations; Checkout would continue the purchase flow without its optional recommendation content. Payment processing retained separate failure and retry rules.

Admission capacity also needed allocation across callers. A product-page concurrency cap below the pool limit could leave connections available for home-page and checkout lookups, provided the cap was enforced before acquisition. The caller-level estimates supplied a starting point, with bursts and occupancy variation included in testing.

Increasing the pool size or adding service instances would permit more database sessions, and both are worth pricing before either is chosen. Raising max_pool_size from 40 to 80 is a one-line configuration change, and it doubles this service’s claim on the database. Adding four instances leaves the per-instance pool alone and has the same effect, because each new instance opens its own pool. Total possible database sessions equal the number of service instances multiplied by the pool size:

\[\text{fleet sessions} = \text{instances} \times \text{pool size}.\]

Twenty instances at 40 is 800 possible sessions. In PostgreSQL the server-wide ceiling is max_connections, which is shared with every other service and with maintenance work, and sessions are not free when idle, since each backend process carries its own memory. So the first check is against the server, not the service:

SHOW max_connections;                  -- server-wide ceiling
SHOW superuser_reserved_connections;  -- reserved, not apps

SELECT usename, application_name, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;

If the database has no session headroom, the team needs a different control. A connection pooler such as PgBouncer in transaction mode lets many application connections share a smaller number of server sessions, which helps precisely when connections are held across think time rather than during queries, and it constrains session-level features such as prepared statements and advisory locks. Reducing occupancy is the other direction, and Chapter 5 takes it up: a cache that answers 60 percent of lookups removes 60 percent of the demand without any new sessions at all. Those additional sessions could also increase lock waits, memory use, or storage contention, so the combined allowances had to fit the shared database’s tested capacity.

If the bounded lookup could not achieve the required recommendation-delivery rate, the next option was precomputed results, which would require a freshness policy and defined cache-miss handling. Recomputing on every miss could recreate the original demand during a cold start.

Page completion and recommendation delivery were measured separately. Successful fallback responses could otherwise conceal a recommendation feature that rarely returned results.

Canary Load and Release Validation

The one-percent rollout at the start of this chapter was a canary release: a small share of production requests exercised the new path before broader exposure. It gave the team evidence about that path at the tested rate. The next calculation shows how much the connection demand would change as exposure increased.

The staging test had verified page construction with only a few concurrent requests. The one-percent canary also exercised a small fraction of the intended connection demand.

At full exposure, product pages were expected to add approximately 395 lookups per second per instance. One-percent exposure contributed about four. Existing callers accounted for 0.35 connections on average, and the canary added approximately

\[3.95 \times 0.070 \approx 0.28.\]

The combined estimate was approximately 0.63 connections.

Connection-load estimates for one 40-connection pool. The higher-rate interval uses the offered rate and an assumed mean occupancy of 70 milliseconds.
Workload Lookups/s Connection load
Existing callers 5 0.35
One-percent exposure \(\approx 9\) \(\approx 0.63\)
Steady full exposure 400 28
Higher-rate interval 560 39.2

The canary could reveal exceptions, incompatible responses, and configuration errors. Its average connection demand provided little evidence about the workload expected at full exposure.

The next load test needed the intended per-instance arrival rate and caller mix. Four observations would determine whether the revised path was ready for another rollout.

The first was the rate the load generator actually sent. A closed-loop generator runs a fixed number of virtual users, each waiting for a response before issuing another request. As responses slow, it sends fewer requests. A test intended to exercise 560 lookups per second might therefore deliver only 300, concealing the effect of the higher offered rate. An open-loop generator schedules arrivals independently of completion, which lets the test maintain offered demand while requests queue. The engineers recorded actual requests and scheduled work that failed to start.6

The second was the response to a fully assigned pool. The test recorded accepted work, completions, rejections, timeouts, and unfinished requests. The engineers checked enforcement of the queue bound and acquisition timeout, along with the response time of fallback pages.

The third was recovery after new lookups stopped. Previously admitted work could continue using connections after the feature flag was disabled. The test measured how long that work took to finish and when page latency returned to its expected range.

The fourth was the distribution across instances. Routing and feature-flag selection could concentrate enabled requests. The engineers repeated the test with uneven routing and fewer service instances while monitoring the shared database.

Each production stage then specified an exposure percentage and an absolute per-instance attempt rate. Before increasing exposure, the release owner compared acquisition time, pending work, page latency, and recommendation delivery with the tested range. Every stop condition had a threshold, an evaluation window, and an action. Sustained acquisition waits outside the tested budget would trigger a return to the preceding stage. If the primary page objective was at risk, the owner would disable the lookup.

The thresholds came from the customer response budget and test results; pool size alone supplies no acquisition-time target. At low traffic, timeout counts and queue measurements supplemented percentile estimates based on few observations.

Approval for further exposure required acceptable recommendation delivery as well as page completion. A low page-error rate could mean that fallback responses worked while most recommendation lookups failed.

Summary

The product-page rollout added a database-backed recommendation call to a request that had previously depended on Catalog Service alone. The interface had been reviewed, but no one had estimated the connections the additional lookups would occupy on each Recommendation Service instance. By the time the page-latency alert fired, the connection pool was fully assigned and callers were waiting to begin their queries.

A release estimate could have exposed the risk before traffic increased. At one-percent exposure, the existing and new lookups used about 0.63 of the 40 connections on average. That result verified the new path under light additional demand; it did not establish how the pool would behave when the feature reached most customers. The team also needed burst tests, acquisition-wait measurements, and a stop threshold connected to the pool rather than to page latency alone.

Baodium restored the product page by allowing it to return without recommendations. Catalog retrieval remained mandatory, while recommendation delivery became a separately measured outcome. The distinction between the page worker and the database connection now becomes important: a worker can be unavailable throughout a remote wait even when no connection has yet been assigned. Chapter 2 applies the same accounting to other finite resources and to the workloads that consume them.

Assumption and scope & The live lookup can satisfy the page-latency objective and recommendation-delivery target at a tested per-instance attempt rate.
Condition that tests it & Feature exposure increases recommendation calls per instance.
Constraint or invariant & Per-instance connection pools use a shared database. The resource budget includes existing callers and the new product-page workload.
Evidence and uncertainty & The initial canary exercised a small fraction of the connection demand associated with the higher-rate interval. Acquisition waits increased when all connections were assigned.

The acceptable per-instance attempt rate under uneven routing, longer occupancy, or loss of a service instance.
Signal and evaluation window & Compare connection acquisition, occupancy, and page latency with the pre-release baseline at each exposure step.
Control and decision & Limit exposure to the validated range. Reconsider live computation if recommendation delivery misses its target at that rate.
Owner and review trigger & The Recommendation Service owner supplies load-test and recovery results. The release owner approves exposure against the recorded thresholds. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.
